Issued at 332 AM CDT Wed Sep 2 2026

Early this morning, broad surface high pressure extends across
the Red River Valley region, with light east-southeast winds
across western and central ND as a lee-side pressure trough
deepens in central MT. Middle- and upper-level flow is in the 
process of starting to turn southwesterly, a process that is 
expected to be complete by this afternoon. GOES nighttime 
microphysics RGB imagery reveals stratus developing in western 
and southern SD, in an area where richer low-level moisture is 
apparent in surface observations. There remains a low to medium
chance that area of stratus will develop and/or advect into 
southwestern ND this morning, with an accompanying low 
probability of fog.

For the better part of today, warm and dry weather is forecast
with highs mainly in the 80s F. Southeast winds will increase
concurrent with a strengthening surface pressure gradient in
western ND, with gusts up to 30 mph expected. Increasing low-
level moisture beneath an EML-related capping inversion will
tend to keep relative humidity values elevated above 30% and
that in turn will mitigate the risk of critical fire weather
conditions. Late afternoon and evening surface dewpoints in the
upper 50s to lower 60s F beneath steep midlevel lapse rates
will contribute to 1500-2000 J/kg of MLCAPE in western ND. This
will yield a low and conditional risk of severe thunderstorms,
though capping at the base of the EML and weak forcing for
ascent lends considerable uncertainty in this scenario. By late
afternoon and evening, a surface warm frontal zone is forecast 
to be in place across eastern MT and western ND, with deep 
boundary layer mixing of a hot and drier air mass in south 
central MT intersecting with that warm frontal zone somewhere 
over southeast or east central MT. In general, low-level 
convergence appears modest near the warm frontal zone, but may 
be somewhat enhanced near the differential mixing zone in 
southeastern MT. That could support isolated deep convective
initiation upstream of southwestern ND, but MLCIN is forecast 
to be greatest in the southwestern ND portion of the surface 
warm frontal zone. Cooler midlevel temperatures in northwestern 
ND will yield lower MLCIN there, but that may be offset by the 
weaker forcing for ascent (e.g., weaker low-level convergence) 
than further southwest. The net result is a broad, 20 percent 
probability of thunderstorms in western ND late this afternoon 
and this evening, with attendant risk of large hail and damaging
winds. Effective-layer shear is on the order of 30 kt, so we 
are messaging quarter size hail as the main hazard, along with 
the possibility of damaging wind gusts to 60 mph given the high-
based nature of any storms that develop. A handful of members 
in the 00z HREF simulated moderate updraft helicity tracks 
across southwestern ND in support of marginal supercell 
structures, so if confidence in convective initiation becomes 
greater in later forecast updates, peak hailstone sizes that we 
message may be increased a bit.

As the boundary layer cools during the evening, we would expect
any evening thunderstorms in western ND to gradually diminish or
become more elevated in nature as they progress eastward. Low-
and midlevel warm air advection is nonetheless forecast to be
ongoing tonight across northwest and central ND, supporting a
low chance of showers and thunderstorms through the night. The
steep lapse rates aloft and further increases in low-level
moisture will result in strong elevated bouyancy (MUCAPE on the
order of 2000-3000 J/kg) tonight in the face of 30-40 kt of 
effective-layer shear even across central ND. Most forecast 
soundings reasonably depict significant CIN for most unstable 
parcels originating around the maximized layer of warm air 
advection near 850 mb, suggesting that overall intensity of any 
overnight convection will be tempered. However, in some cases, 
the depth of the moist layer becomes sufficient in forecast 
soundings to reduce CIN for the layers that possess the large 
bouyancy. While the overall setting of weak synoptic-scale 
ascent, a warm EML aloft, and lack of CAM-based signals for 
robust storms overnight tends to suggest the risk of strong to 
severe storms will be minimized in central and northwestern ND 
overnight, a low and very conditional risk of an isolated severe
storm even across central ND is apparent if the moist layer 
ends up deeper than the consensus of guidance expects.

A low to medium chance of showers and thunderstorms continues
Thursday and into Thursday evening in north central and into
eastern ND, including the James River Valley, both due to
early-day warm air advection aloft, and large bouyancy in the
afternoon and early evening. Once again, forcing for ascent is
